segments.text: Physical geology studies the Earth’s materials and the processes that shape its surface — the foundation on which every later, more specialised chapter in this subject builds.

blocks.text: 1. Origin and age of Earth; internal structure

segments.text: The Earth formed roughly 4.6 billion years ago through the accretion of material within the early solar system’s protoplanetary disk; this age is established primarily through radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest terrestrial rocks. Volcanic activity is heavily concentrated along plate boundaries (Chapter 4), particularly subduction zones and mid-ocean ridges, connecting this topic directly to the plate tectonics framework developed later in this Paper.

blocks.text: 5. Work of rivers, groundwater, glaciers, wind, and oceans

segments.text: Each of these agents both erodes and deposits characteristic landforms:

segments.text: studies the origin and evolution of landforms as the product of the interacting processes above, acting over geological time on the underlying rock structure — the same landform-forming agents produce systematically different results depending on climate, rock type, and tectonic setting, which is why a process–landform framework (recognising which agent and process combination produced a given feature) is a more useful study approach than memorising landforms in isolation.

items.text: The Earth’s layered internal structure (crust, mantle, core) was established largely through seismic wave behaviour, particularly the absence of S-waves in the liquid outer core.
Volcanic eruption style depends on magma composition (viscosity and gas content), and both volcanoes and earthquakes concentrate heavily along plate boundaries.
Weathering (in-place breakdown) is distinct from erosion (removal and transport); mass wasting is gravity-driven downslope movement, distinct from both.
Rivers, groundwater, glaciers, wind, and oceans each have characteristic erosional and depositional landforms, determined by their specific mode of action.
Geomorphology is best studied through a process–landform framework, since the same agents produce different results depending on climate, rock type, and tectonic setting.
